opus-5.5.text:
I think integration is really essential, and honestly it's something I've come to appreciate more and more over time. For a long while the field tended to swing like a pendulum: there was the era of symbolic, logic-based approaches to reasoning, then the statistical and neural era where many people felt we could just learn everything from data, and now with large language models some feel scale alone will get us there. My view is that each of these perspectives captured something real, and the most interesting progress happens when we combine their strengths rather than treating them as competing camps.

Take commonsense reasoning, which I've worked on for years. Neural models are remarkably good at picking up the fuzzy, intuitive, context-dependent patterns of everyday knowledge, the kind of thing that was really brittle when people tried to hand-code it with logic rules. But at the same time, these models can be inconsistent, they can hallucinate, and they don't always respect the kind of structure and constraints that reasoning requires. So ideas from the symbolic tradition, like explicit knowledge representations, constraints, or structured search over possible inferences, can be very useful when layered on top of, or interleaved with, neural generation. Some of our work on things like knowledge graphs generated by language models, or decoding algorithms that enforce logical constraints, came out of exactly that kind of thinking.

And I'd go beyond just neural plus symbolic. I think we should be drawing from cognitive science, from developmental psychology, from philosophy, and from linguistics, because humans reason in ways that are not purely deductive. We do abductive reasoning, we reason about intentions and social norms, we reason with incomplete information. Understanding how people actually do that gives us better hypotheses about what our systems are missing.

The other piece is that integration also means being open-minded about methodology. Sometimes a smaller model with a clever algorithm or better data can outperform a much larger model on certain reasoning tasks. That tells us scale is one ingredient, but not the whole recipe. So I try to encourage my students to not just follow the dominant trend, but to ask what's fundamentally missing and borrow ideas from wherever they might come from. That's where I think the genuine breakthroughs in artificial reasoning are going to happen.

r001.rationale: The response advocates combining and layering research approaches, but it does not characterize artificial reasoning as a systems-level orchestration problem or say that components must be coordinated in the right sequence.

fable-5.1.text:
Guest: Thanks so much for having me, Sam. So I actually think this is one of the most important questions for the field right now, because for a long time we've had this kind of pendulum swinging between camps. You had the symbolic AI tradition, which was all about logic, knowledge representation, formal reasoning, and then you had the neural, statistical tradition, which is really about learning patterns from data. And historically those communities didn't talk to each other very much. People were almost tribal about it.

My own view is that reasoning, at least the kind of reasoning humans do, is not purely one or the other. If you think about how people actually reason, it's incredibly intuitive and fast and messy. We make inferences about what someone meant, or what's going to happen next, in a split second, without consciously running through anything that looks like a logical proof. That part feels very neural, very pattern-based. But then there's also a slower, more deliberate component, where you check yourself, you consider alternatives, you notice that something doesn't add up. That part has a more structured, almost symbolic flavor.

So when I think about building artificial reasoning, I don't see it as a matter of picking the winner. I see it as asking, what is each approach actually good at, and what are its failure modes? Large language models are remarkable at the intuitive, associative side. They've absorbed an enormous amount of commonsense from text, and they can produce plausible inferences very fluently. But they're also surprisingly brittle. They'll make a basic error about physical or social commonsense that a child wouldn't make, and they're often not able to tell you when they're uncertain. And that's precisely where ideas from the symbolic world, about consistency, about structured knowledge, about verification and search, can come in and help.

The work we've done on things like commonsense knowledge graphs, or using neural models to generate structured knowledge rather than hand-writing it, is really an attempt to live in that middle ground. We're saying, let the neural model do what it does well, which is generalize and cover the long tail of situations nobody wrote down, but give it a structure that lets us inspect what it believes, test it for contradictions, and compose inferences in a more reliable way.

I'd also add that integration shouldn't stop at symbolic versus neural. I've found a lot of inspiration from cognitive science and from philosophy, and even from the social sciences, because so much of reasoning is about people, about norms, intentions, what's appropriate in a given context. If we only build on the computational traditions and ignore what those other fields understand about how humans think and judge, we end up with systems that are powerful but kind of hollow. So for me the role of integration is really about intellectual humility. No single community has figured out reasoning, and the interesting progress tends to happen at the seams between them.

r001.rationale: The response advocates combining neural and symbolic methods and describes neural generation followed by structuring, inspection, and verification. It does not clearly characterize artificial reasoning as a systems-level orchestration problem requiring components to be coordinated in the right sequence.

astra-6.text:
I think integration is really important, because reasoning is such a broad capability that it’s unlikely any single approach will give us everything we need. Learning from data helps us recognize patterns and generalize, while more structured approaches can help us express constraints and check whether a conclusion actually follows from the premises.

The interesting question is how to make these approaches work together. Can a model learn useful abstractions from examples and then apply them consistently in a new situation? Can it use knowledge about the world while also recognizing when that knowledge is insufficient?

I also think we need a connection between building systems and understanding their failures. When a system gets an answer right, we should ask what happens if we change one small assumption. That can help us distinguish a useful pattern it has learned from reasoning that holds up across situations. So integration, to me, is about letting different approaches inform and challenge one another.

r001.rationale: The response says different approaches should work together and gives an example of learning abstractions before applying them, but it does not characterize development as a systems-level orchestration problem requiring components to be coordinated in the right sequence.

sol-6.1.text:
I think integrating different approaches is essential, because reasoning is not one single capability. Some situations call for learning from examples, others require explicit rules, and others require commonsense knowledge about how the world works. We want systems that can bring those capabilities together.

The interesting question is how to make those approaches inform one another. Can learned models help us acquire knowledge, while more structured reasoning helps us check whether their conclusions are consistent? I think we should remain open to that combination, rather than assume that one approach will solve everything.

r001.rationale: The response says different approaches should be combined and inform one another, but it does not characterize development as coordinating components in the right sequence.
